questions.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=1
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=6\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=1.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

questions.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=9{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=5
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=10\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-7.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & -16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-7)I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}]+7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=7.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=7
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $3{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}=24?$
questions.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ -3 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -24 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-6\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $4{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2} & =24 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{6}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{6})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt{6}$ and $2.$
